newsitem.title: UK: Britain starts millennium countdown at Greenwich.
newsitem.headline: Britain starts millennium countdown at Greenwich.

text.p: Britain began the countdown to the next millennium on Saturday with a clock on the Greenwich Meridian Line ticking off the 1,000 remaining days until the year 2000.
The clock, sited on the wall of the Royal Observatory in Greenwich which became the world time standard in 1884, is designed to be precise to the nearest millionth of a second.
It started the 1,000-day countdown to December 31 1999 at the stroke of midnight to the sound of champagne corks and fireworks.
Some mathematicians said the clock was inaccurate because it did not take account of a "leap second" which is to be introduced between 23.59.59 and midnight on June 30 this year.
But Dr Kristen Lippincott, director of the Millennium Project at the National Maritime Museum, dismissed the critics.
"Our clock is accurate. It will be wrong to take account of these leap seconds until they are inserted. Before then, they simply do not exist," she said.
Leap seconds are added to the time every few years to compensate for minute variations in the earth's rotation.
